question: What allows the commander to decide whether a flight may start with an item unserviceable?

options.text: The MEL in the operations manual

explanation: The minimum equipment list, included in the operations manual, allows the commander to decide whether a flight may start or continue from an intermediate stop with an item unserviceable.

question: What must the aeroplane's instruments allow the crew to do?

options.text: Navigate without any ground aids anywhere in the world
Fly with only one pilot in all conditions
Control the flight path and keep within limits

explanation: An aeroplane must have instruments that let the crew control the flight path, carry out any required procedural manoeuvres and observe the aeroplane's operating limitations.

question: Above how many passenger seats must an aeroplane have a lockable flight deck door?
explanation: Aeroplanes with more than 19 passenger seats must have a lockable door between the passenger compartment and the flight deck, marked crew only.

question: A door or curtain must be passed through in an emergency. What is required?

options.text: That it is removed before every flight
A means to hold it open, and a placard
That it is locked for take-off and landing
That it is made of transparent material

explanation: Doors or curtains on an emergency route must have a means of securing them open and signs indicating they must be secured open for take-off and landing.

question: Passengers can lock a toilet door. What must the crew have?

options.text: A key to every passenger's luggage
A list of who is using the toilet

explanation: The crew must have a means of unlocking any door that can be locked by passengers.

question: How many first aid kits are needed for 150 passenger seats?
explanation: First aid kits: 0–99 seats 1; 100–199 seats 2; 200–299 seats 3; 300 or more 4.

question: How many first aid kits are needed for 320 passenger seats?
explanation: 300 or more seats require 4 first aid kits.

question: When must an emergency medical kit be carried?

options.text: Over 30 passengers and 60 min or more from medical help
More than 100 passengers and a flight planned to last over 3 hours
Only on flights over the sea, whatever the size

explanation: An emergency medical kit, for use by doctors or other qualified people, is required in aeroplanes authorised to carry more than 30 passengers if any point of the flight is 60 minutes or more from qualified medical help.

question: Where should the emergency medical kit preferably be carried?

options.text: On the flight deck, under security conditions
In the cargo hold, in a locked and fireproof container

explanation: The emergency medical kit must be dust and moisture proof and carried under security conditions, preferably on the flight deck.

question: Above what altitude must a pressurised aeroplane carrying required cabin crew have first aid oxygen?
explanation: A pressurised aeroplane above 25 000 ft with required cabin crew must carry undiluted first aid oxygen for passengers who may need it after a depressurisation.

question: For what proportion of passengers must first aid oxygen be provided?

options.text: One person for each cabin crew member on board
At least 2%, and never less than one person

explanation: First aid oxygen is calculated for at least 2% of passengers carried, but in no case for less than one person, at an average 3 litres/minute/person, for the time cabin altitude is between 8000 and 15 000 ft.

question: What is the minimum number of first aid oxygen dispensing units?
explanation: There must be sufficient dispensing units, but in no case fewer than two, which may be portable.

question: What minimum mass flow must first aid oxygen equipment deliver to each user?
explanation: The equipment must be able to deliver at least 4 litres per minute STPD to each user; means may be provided to reduce it to not less than 2 litres per minute.

question: What colour are fuselage break-in markings?

options.text: Red or yellow, outlined in white if needed

explanation: Areas suitable for break-in are marked with red or yellow lines, outlined in white if needed for contrast.

question: If the corner break-in markings are more than 2 m apart, what is added?

options.text: A continuous line all round the area
A painted arrow pointing to the door
Intermediate lines 20 cm × 5 cm every 3 m
Extra 9 cm × 3 cm lines, no gap over 2 m

explanation: If the corners are more than 2 m apart, intermediate 9 cm × 3 cm lines are added so there is no more than 2 m between adjacent markings.

question: Above what sill height must an emergency exit have a means of reaching the ground?
explanation: Where the sill is more than 1.83 m above the ground with the gear extended (or after a gear collapse), a means of reaching the ground, such as a slide, must be fitted.

question: When need an overwing exit not have a descent device?

options.text: When the aircraft has fewer than 50 seats
When the route ends below 1.83 m
When the exit is behind the wing
When the exit is only used in ditching

explanation: A device need not be fitted to overwing exits if the exit route ends at a point less than 1.83 m above the ground.

question: Why must aircraft carry a cockpit voice recorder?

options.text: To help investigate accidents and incidents
To monitor crew performance on routine flights

explanation: CVRs record communications and flight deck sounds that are often vital evidence in investigating an incident or accident.

question: An aeroplane over 5700 kg had its CofA issued between 1998 and 2020. What minimum CVR recording time applies?
explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg first certificated on or after 1 April 1998 need a CVR recording at least the last 2 hours. Older ones need at least 30 minutes. Large aeroplanes certificated more recently need longer, see below.

question: A new aeroplane over 27 000 kg received its first CofA in 2022. What minimum CVR recording time applies under current rules?
explanation: Under current rules, aeroplanes with a maximum certificated take-off mass over 27 000 kg first certificated on or after 1 January 2021 must record at least the last 25 hours on the CVR; others 2 hours.

question: An older aeroplane (CofA before April 1998) over 5700 kg must have a CVR recording at least how long?
explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg with a CofA issued before 1 April 1998 must record at least the last 30 minutes.

question: Which smaller aeroplanes certificated between 1990 and 1998 also need a CVR?

options.text: Any aeroplane with more than 4 seats
Any aeroplane flown by a single pilot, whatever its engines

explanation: From 1 January 1990, multi-engine turbine aeroplanes under 5700 kg with more than 9 passenger seats were included, recording at least 30 minutes.

question: When must the CVR start recording?

options.text: When the pilot switches it on after take-off, at 1000 ft
At engine start, by the pilot
Automatically before first moving under own power
At the start of the take-off roll

explanation: CVRs must switch on automatically before the aeroplane first moves under its own power and record until the end of the flight.

question: What device must flight recorders have to help recovery after a crash at sea?

options.text: A parachute that opens on impact

explanation: Flight recorders must meet crashworthiness and fire protection standards and be fitted with a device to assist underwater location.

question: What colour are flight recorders, despite being called "black boxes"?
explanation: Flight data recorders are usually painted a bright (Day-Glo) red or yellow to help find them.

question: What does a flight data recorder record?

options.text: Data on systems, control positions and performance
Only the flight crew's voices and all radio calls made

explanation: FDRs record data on aeroplane systems, control positions and performance parameters.

question: What minimum recording period must a flight data recorder normally retain?

options.text: The last 100 hours of operation, on a loop

explanation: An FDR must retain at least the last 25 hours of operation; for aeroplanes of 5700 kg or less this may be reduced to 10 hours.

question: For aeroplanes of 5700 kg or less that need an FDR, to what may the recording period be reduced?
explanation: For aeroplanes with a maximum certificated take-off mass of 5700 kg or less, the FDR period may be reduced to 10 hours.

question: Which aeroplanes certificated on or after 1 April 1998 need a digital FDR?

options.text: All aeroplanes with more than 2 seats, whatever the engine type
Multi-turbines over 9 seats, or any over 5700 kg

explanation: From 1 April 1998, multi-engine turbine aeroplanes with more than 9 passenger seats, or any aeroplane over 5700 kg, need a digital FDR.

question: Which instrument is required for day VFR flight?
explanation: Day VFR requires a magnetic compass, accurate timepiece, sensitive altimeter, ASI, VSI, turn and slip or turn coordinator, attitude indicator, stabilised direction indicator and OAT indicator.

question: What must the timepiece required for flight show?
explanation: An accurate timepiece showing hours, minutes and seconds is required.

question: In which units must the outside air temperature indicator be calibrated?
explanation: A means of indicating the outside air temperature in degrees Celsius is required on the flight deck.

question: For short local VFR flights, which instruments may be replaced by a turn and slip indicator?

options.text: The turn and slip, attitude and direction indicators
The VSI and the OAT gauge, plus the clock and compass

explanation: For flights up to 60 minutes, taking off and landing at the same aerodrome and staying within 50 NM, the turn indicator, attitude indicator and direction indicator may be replaced by a turn and slip indicator, or a turn coordinator with slip, or an attitude and slip indicator.

question: What conditions allow simplified instruments for a local VFR flight?

options.text: Up to 30 minutes, any aerodrome, within 25 NM
Up to 60 minutes, same aerodrome, within 50 NM
Any flight by day in CAVOK conditions
Up to 90 minutes, same aerodrome, within 100 NM

explanation: The simplification applies to flights not exceeding 60 minutes, taking off and landing at the same aerodrome and remaining within 50 NM.

question: When two pilots are required, what must the second pilot's station have?

options.text: No instruments, as the commander flies
Only a repeater of the commander's displays on one screen
Its own full set of basic flight instruments

explanation: The second pilot's station needs separate instruments: altimeter, airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator, turn and slip (or coordinator), attitude indicator and stabilised direction indicator.

question: Which aeroplanes need a heated pitot tube even for VFR?

options.text: Only those with jet engines, whatever their mass
Over 5700 kg or 9 seats, or certificated after April 1999

explanation: Heated pitot (or equivalent) is required for aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats, and for those first certificated on or after 1 April 1999.

question: When must an aeroplane have a Machmeter at each pilot station?

options.text: When it carries more than 100 passengers at high altitude
When it has more than two engines
When it has Mach limits not shown on the ASI

explanation: Aeroplanes with compressibility limitations not otherwise indicated by the airspeed indicators need a Mach number indicator at each pilot's station.

question: What is needed for each flight crew member on duty, even for day VFR?

options.text: A portable oxygen bottle and full-face mask

explanation: Day VFR operations require a headset with boom microphone or equivalent for each flight crew member on flight deck duty.

question: Which instrument must be added to the day VFR list for IFR or night VFR?
explanation: IFR or night VFR adds a standby altimeter, a heated pitot system (with failure warning for larger newer aircraft), two independent static systems and an illuminated chart holder.

question: For IFR, what static system is required on a propeller aeroplane of 5700 kg or less?

options.text: One static system plus an alternate source
Two independent static systems, with no alternate source

explanation: Two independent static systems are required, except that propeller aeroplanes of 5700 kg or less may have one static system and an alternate static source.

question: For IFR, what must larger aeroplanes certificated after 1 April 1998 have for the pitot heater?

options.text: A manual valve to drain the pitot
A warning of pitot heater failure

explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 seats certificated since 1 April 1998 need a warning indication of pitot heater failure.

question: What must a single-pilot IFR aeroplane have?

options.text: A second pilot station with its own full set of instruments
An autopilot with altitude hold and heading mode

explanation: Aeroplanes operated under IFR with a single pilot must have an autopilot with at least altitude hold and heading mode.

question: Which aeroplanes need an altitude alerting system?
explanation: An altitude alerting system is required for turbojet aeroplanes, and turboprops over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats.

question: What must an altitude alerting system do?

options.text: Level the aircraft automatically at the selected altitude
Alert near a set altitude, and aurally on leaving it
Show the altitude of other traffic

explanation: It must alert the crew on approaching a preselected altitude, and by at least an aural signal when deviating from it.

question: For how long must the standby attitude indicator work after total failure of normal electrical generation?
explanation: The standby attitude indicator must operate reliably for at least 30 minutes after total failure of the normal electrical generating system.

question: Which aeroplanes need a standby attitude indicator usable from either pilot station?

options.text: Only aeroplanes over 27 000 kg flying above FL290
Over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats

explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats must have a standby attitude indicator usable from either pilot's station.

question: How must the standby attitude indicator start working after a total electrical generation failure?

options.text: When the crew deploy the ram air turbine
When the pilot selects battery power

explanation: It must become operative automatically after total failure of the normal electrical generating system, and show when it is on its own power.

question: Which lights are required for day flight?
explanation: By day an aeroplane needs a functioning anti-collision light system, lighting for essential instruments and equipment, cabin lighting and a torch at each crew station.

question: What additional lights are required for night operation?

options.text: Navigation lights and two landing lights
Wing inspection lights and logo lights only

explanation: At night aeroplanes additionally need navigation/position lights and two landing lights.

question: What must be readily accessible at each crew member station?
explanation: A torch readily accessible at each crew member station is required.

question: When is a flight considered "over water" for life jacket requirements?

options.text: More than 100 NM from shore only, whatever the departure route
Over 50 NM from shore, or take-off/approach over water

explanation: Over-water rules apply when the aeroplane is more than 93 km (50 NM) from shore, or when the take-off or approach path is over water.

question: What must each life jacket be equipped with?

options.text: A whistle and a mirror only

explanation: Each life jacket or equivalent flotation device must be equipped with a location light and be stowed within easy reach of its user's seat.

question: An aeroplane able to continue to an aerodrome after critical engine failure flies over water. Beyond what distance from land must it carry life rafts?

options.text: 120 minutes at cruising speed or 400 NM, whichever is more
30 minutes at cruising speed or 100 NM, whichever is less
120 minutes at cruising speed or 400 NM, whichever is less
60 minutes at cruising speed or 200 NM, whichever is less

explanation: For aeroplanes able to continue after critical engine failure, rafts and ELTs are needed beyond 120 minutes at cruising speed or 400 NM from land, whichever is less.

question: For other aeroplanes, beyond what distance from land must life rafts be carried?

options.text: 15 minutes or 50 NM, whichever is less
30 min at cruise speed or 100 NM, if less
120 minutes or 400 NM, whichever is less
60 minutes or 200 NM, whichever is less

explanation: For all other aeroplanes the limit is 30 minutes at cruising speed or 100 NM, whichever is less.

question: How much life raft capacity is required on a long overwater flight?

options.text: Enough for all, even with the biggest raft lost
Enough for half the people on board
One raft for each cabin crew member, placed at the exits

explanation: Rafts must carry everyone on board; unless excess rafts are provided, the overload capacity must accommodate everyone if the largest raft is lost.

question: How many survival ELTs must be carried on a long overwater flight requiring rafts?
explanation: At least two survival ELTs, transmitting on 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz, must be carried.

question: On which frequencies does a survival ELT transmit?
explanation: ELTs transmit on 121.5 MHz (homing) and 406 MHz (satellite data). Note that 406 is in megahertz, not kilohertz.

question: When must a pressurised passenger aeroplane have serviceable weather radar?

options.text: When detectable hazardous weather is expected en route
Only over the sea, when out of radar coverage

explanation: Pressurised aeroplanes carrying passengers need serviceable weather radar when thunderstorms or other hazardous weather detectable by radar are expected along the route.

question: Which unpressurised aeroplanes also need weather radar in such conditions?

options.text: Those over 5700 kg or with more than 9 seats
All single-engine aeroplanes flying in IMC

explanation: The requirement extends to unpressurised aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats.

question: What may a small pressurised propeller aeroplane use instead of weather radar?

options.text: Nothing; it must have a fully serviceable weather radar

explanation: Pressurised propeller aeroplanes up to 5700 kg with no more than 9 seats may use another suitable system for detecting thunderstorms and hazardous conditions.

question: At night in icing conditions, what must an aeroplane certified for icing have?

options.text: An ice detector or ice lighting
A second de-icing system on the wings and tail

explanation: Aeroplanes operated in icing at night need an ice detection device or a means of illumination to detect ice formation.

question: Who is responsible for terrain clearance, except when ATC is radar vectoring?
explanation: ATC does not accept responsibility for terrain clearance except during radar vectoring; the responsibility rests with the pilots.

question: Which of these does a GPWS warn of?
explanation: GPWS gives aural and visual warnings of excessive sink rate, ground proximity, altitude loss after take-off or go-around, incorrect landing configuration and downward glide slope deviation.

question: What does TAWS (enhanced GPWS) add to a basic GPWS?

options.text: A weather radar picture overlaid on the map display

explanation: TAWS adds predictive terrain hazard warning with a forward-looking capability, a terrain display and a terrain clearance floor.

question: Which aeroplanes must have TAWS?

options.text: Turbines over 5700 kg or over 9 seats
Only jets flying on international routes

explanation: TAWS is required for turbine-powered commercial aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats.

question: Which aeroplanes must have ACAS II?

options.text: Turbines over 5700 kg or over 19 seats
Only aeroplanes flying above FL290 in RVSM airspace

explanation: All turbine-powered aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 19 passenger seats must be equipped with ACAS II.

question: An ACAS RA conflicts with an ATC instruction. What must the pilot do?

options.text: Ignore both and keep the current level and heading
Follow the RA smoothly and immediately

explanation: Pilots must respond smoothly and immediately to ACAS RAs, even if this conflicts with ATC instructions.

question: How many radio transceivers must a commercial aeroplane carry at least?
explanation: Provision must be made for unserviceabilities, so at least 2 transceivers must be carried, able to communicate with ATC and receive weather, including on 121.5 MHz.

question: For an oceanic flight, what radio fit is typical?

options.text: At least one VHF and one HF
One satellite telephone only, for the whole crossing

explanation: In practice, 2 VHF transceivers are needed for domestic airspace and at least 1 VHF and 1 HF for oceanic flight.

question: Above how many passenger seats is a public address system required?
explanation: Aeroplanes with more than 19 passenger seats must have a public address system and a crew interphone.

question: An aeroplane with 15 seats has an MTOM of 18 000 kg. Does it need a crew interphone?

options.text: Yes, because its MTOM exceeds 15 000 kg
Only if it carries cabin crew on long flights
Only if it flies above FL250
No, because it has fewer than 20 seats

explanation: A crew interphone is also required for aeroplanes with 19 seats or fewer if the MTOM exceeds 15 000 kg.

question: What must be available to each required flight crew member under IFR?

options.text: A separate transponder for each pilot station

explanation: An aeroplane may not be operated under IFR unless an audio selector panel is accessible to each required flight crew member.

question: What alert threshold must RVSM equipment use for a deviation from the selected level?
explanation: The altitude alert threshold for RVSM must not exceed ±90 m (300 ft).

question: Which navigation receivers are required at least for IFR or night VFR?
explanation: At least VOR, ADF and DME are required, plus RNAV, ILS, MLS or marker receivers where needed. Where navigation relies on one aid alone, that equipment must be duplicated.

question: When must VOR, ADF or DME equipment be duplicated?

options.text: Only for single-pilot operations under IFR at night
When navigation relies on that aid alone

explanation: The requirement for VOR/DME/ADF is doubled where navigation is based on that aid alone.

question: How must communication and navigation equipment be installed?

options.text: So one failure does not cause another
In one rack, close together, for easy maintenance
All on a single power bus

explanation: The installation must be such that failure of any single unit for communication or navigation does not cause failure of another such unit.

subtopic: Fuses, wipers and items not needing approval
question: What spare fuses must be carried where fuses can be replaced in flight?

options.text: One complete set of every fuse
20% of each rating, and at least 5 of each type carried
10% of each rating, and at least 3 of each
5% of each rating, at least 1 of each

explanation: There must be at least 10% of each type and rating of fuse, with not less than 3 of each.

subtopic: Fuses, wipers and items not needing approval
question: Above what MTOM are windshield wipers (or equivalent) required at each pilot station?
explanation: Windshield wipers or equivalent are required at each pilot station if the MTOM exceeds 5700 kg.

subtopic: Fuses, wipers and items not needing approval
question: Which of these items does not need an equipment approval?
explanation: Items not requiring approval include fuses, torches, timepieces, chart holders, first aid and emergency medical kits, megaphones, survival and pyrotechnic equipment, and child restraint devices.

question: From what age must a person on board have their own seat or berth?
explanation: A seat or berth must be provided for each person aged over two; infants may use approved child restraint devices.

question: What must each flight crew seat have?

options.text: A four-point harness with no inertia reel

explanation: Flight crew seats must have a safety belt and shoulder harness with a device to automatically restrain the occupant in sudden deceleration.

question: How must belts with shoulder harnesses be released?

options.text: With a single point of release
With two separate buckles, one for each shoulder

explanation: All safety belts with shoulder harnesses must have a single point of release.

question: At or below what MTOM is the diagonal shoulder strap not needed on crew seats?
explanation: Up to 5700 kg, crew seats may have belts with a diagonal shoulder strap instead of a full harness; up to 2730 kg the diagonal strap is not needed.

question: When must "fasten seat belts" and "no smoking" signs be fitted?

options.text: Only on aeroplanes over 5700 kg carrying cabin crew
When passengers cannot be seen from the flight deck

explanation: Aeroplanes in which the passenger seating is not visible from the flight deck must have signs to tell passengers and cabin crew when to fasten belts and when smoking is not allowed.

question: In a pressurised aeroplane, for how long must oxygen be provided for flight deck crew on duty?

options.text: 10 minutes after any depressurisation, whatever the altitude
Above 13 000 ft always; above 10 000 ft after 30 min

explanation: Flight deck occupants on duty need oxygen for all time when cabin altitude exceeds 13 000 ft, and for time above 10 000 ft (up to 13 000 ft) after the first 30 minutes, subject to minimum quantities.

question: What is the minimum flight crew oxygen supply for a pressurised aeroplane certificated above 25 000 ft?
explanation: The minimum is 30 minutes for aeroplanes certificated to fly no higher than 25 000 ft, and 2 hours for those certificated above 25 000 ft, with quick-donning masks.

question: What masks must flight crew have in aeroplanes certificated above 25 000 ft?
explanation: Aeroplanes certificated to fly above 25 000 ft must have quick-donning masks for the flight crew.

question: In a pressurised aeroplane, above what cabin altitude must oxygen be available for 100% of passengers?
explanation: 100% of passengers need oxygen for all time above 15 000 ft cabin altitude, but in no case less than 10 minutes.

question: In a pressurised aeroplane, for what proportion of passengers is oxygen needed between 14 000 and 15 000 ft cabin altitude?
explanation: 30% of passengers need oxygen for the whole time cabin altitude is between 14 000 and 15 000 ft.

question: In a pressurised aeroplane, for what proportion of passengers is oxygen needed between 10 000 and 14 000 ft after the first 30 minutes?
explanation: 10% of passengers need oxygen for the time above 10 000 ft (up to 14 000 ft) after the first 30 minutes.

question: What descent profile sets the minimum 30-minute crew oxygen supply?

options.text: To 10 000 ft in 10 min, then 20 min level
Descent to 10 000 ft in 4 minutes, then 26 minutes level
Descent to sea level in 30 minutes

explanation: The 30-minute supply is the oxygen needed for a constant-rate descent from maximum certificated altitude to 10 000 ft in 10 minutes followed by 20 minutes at 10 000 ft. The 2-hour supply assumes 110 minutes at 10 000 ft.

question: What descent profile sets the minimum 10-minute passenger oxygen supply?

options.text: Descent to 10 000 ft in 10 minutes, then 20 minutes level
Descent from maximum altitude to 15 000 ft in 10 minutes

explanation: The 10-minute minimum for 100% of passengers is the oxygen needed for a constant-rate descent from maximum certificated altitude to 15 000 ft in 10 minutes.

question: For the oxygen tables, do infants count as passengers?

options.text: Only in unpressurised aeroplanes flying above 10 000 ft

explanation: For these tables, "passengers" means passengers actually carried and includes infants.

question: In an unpressurised aeroplane, when must flight deck crew on duty have oxygen?
explanation: In unpressurised aeroplanes, flight deck occupants on duty need oxygen for the entire time above 10 000 ft.

question: In an unpressurised aeroplane, above what altitude must oxygen be provided for 100% of passengers?
explanation: 100% of passengers need oxygen for all time above 13 000 ft, and 10% after 30 minutes between 10 000 and 13 000 ft.

question: In an unpressurised aeroplane, for what share of passengers is oxygen needed after 30 minutes between 10 000 and 13 000 ft?
explanation: 10% of passengers need oxygen for the time after 30 minutes between 10 000 and 13 000 ft.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: Which aeroplanes need protective breathing equipment (PBE) for the crew?

options.text: Over 5700 kg or with more than 19 seats
Only aeroplanes with a Class A or B cargo hold

explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 19 seats need crew PBE.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: For how long must crew protective breathing equipment provide oxygen?
explanation: Flight crew and cabin crew PBE must protect eyes, nose and mouth and provide oxygen for at least 15 minutes.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: Where must cabin crew PBE be installed?

options.text: Next to each cabin crew duty station
In one central locker near the forward galley

explanation: Cabin crew PBE must be installed adjacent to each cabin crew member's duty station.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: Where must portable PBE be stowed for a Class A or B cargo compartment?

options.text: Outside the compartment, next to its entrance
Inside the compartment, clipped to the wall

explanation: For a cargo compartment the PBE must be stowed outside, adjacent to the entrance.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: Which aeroplanes must have a crash axe or crowbar on the flight deck?

options.text: Over 5700 kg or with more than 9 seats
All aeroplanes with a flight deck door
Only those with more than 200 seats

explanation: Aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 9 passenger seats must have a crash axe or crowbar on the flight deck.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: Above how many passenger seats must an extra crash axe or crowbar be carried in the rear galley?
explanation: Aeroplanes with more than 200 passenger seats need an additional crash axe or crowbar stowed in the rearmost galley, out of passengers' sight.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: How many megaphones does a single-deck aeroplane with 150 passenger seats need?
explanation: Megaphones per deck: 61–99 seats 1; 100 or more 2. Aeroplanes with 60 seats or fewer need none.

subtopic: Protective breathing equipment and emergency tools
question: How many megaphones does an aeroplane with 80 passenger seats need?
explanation: 61–99 passenger seats require one megaphone.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: What must power the emergency lighting?

options.text: An independent source, working after battery switch-off
The main aircraft batteries, through the emergency bus

explanation: Emergency lighting must have an independent power source that provides power after the aircraft batteries have been switched off.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: Which of these is a source of emergency lighting?

options.text: Reading lights in each seat, switched on by the crew
Floor-level exit lights and exit signs

explanation: Emergency lighting includes general cabin illumination, floor-level exit area lighting, illuminated exit markings and signs, and exterior lighting at overwing exits and exits with descent devices.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: An aeroplane with more than 19 seats first certificated after 1 July 2008 needs which ELTs?

options.text: Three ELTs of any type, all portable
Two ELTs, one of them automatic

explanation: Aeroplanes with more than 19 seats need one automatic ELT or two of any type; those first certificated after 1 July 2008 need two ELTs, one automatic.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: An aeroplane with 12 seats, first certificated in 2010, needs which ELT?
explanation: Aeroplanes with up to 19 seats need one ELT of any type, or one automatic ELT if first certificated after 1 July 2008.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: What is the 406 MHz ELT signal used for?
explanation: 121.5 MHz is used for homing; 406 MHz carries the data detected by search and rescue satellites.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: What must aeroplanes carry over areas where search and rescue would be especially difficult?

options.text: Pyrotechnics, an ELT and route survival kit
A satellite telephone only, kept on the flight deck

explanation: Over areas where SAR would be especially difficult, aeroplanes need pyrotechnic signalling equipment, at least one ELT and additional survival equipment for the route.

subtopic: Emergency lighting, ELTs and survival equipment
question: Within what distance may an aeroplane able to continue after critical engine failure fly without extra survival equipment, where SAR is not especially difficult?

options.text: 30 minutes at cruising speed, all engines operating

explanation: Extra equipment is not needed if SAR is not especially difficult and the aeroplane stays within 120 minutes at the one-engine-out cruising speed (for those able to continue after critical engine failure), 30 minutes at cruising speed for others, or 90 minutes for large transport aeroplanes.
